name: England and Wales
subtitle: The land that became England and Wales, 4000 BCE – 1625 CE
scopeNote: This map shows the land that became England and Wales. For most of the period neither existed: 'England' as a single kingdom dates only from the 10th century (Aethelstan, 927), and Wales was a land of separate kingdoms until the conquest of 1282-3. Earlier names, peoples and borders are shown as they stood at each date; borders were zones rather than lines, and the outlines drawn are indicative.

woodland.note: Only two points are anchored. Rackham estimated that half of England had been cleared by about 500 BCE, and that woodland and wood-pasture covered about 15% of the land recorded in Domesday Book (1086); Domesday omits the far north, and the average hides big regional differences. For 1350 secondary accounts of Rackham give between about 6% and 10%; 8% is used. Everything else is interpolation: the early Neolithic 'wildwood' was not a closed canopy everywhere and 75% is a convention; Roman-period and post-Roman values (including a modest regrowth after 400) are guesses; the 1625 figure assumes little net change after the Black Death. The trend is for England; Wales was more wooded at most dates.
